name: Umar Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for taking the time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior associate in the litigation team at a big regional firm, so I work on court disputes, mostly building companies arguing about late or faulty work. Honestly, a lot of my day is disclosure, which means going through thousands of emails and site reports to find the ones that matter for the case. The rest is drafting letters to the other side and preparing bundles for hearings. The bit I like is going to court with the partner and watching the barrister use something I found.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The disclosure, after about four in the afternoon, when every email about concrete looks the same. I'm not the sharpest at spotting the important document, my supervisor Graham has told me that twice. I use the firm's review software with the AI search now and then, when Graham says it's fine for that case. Outside work I live alone in a rented studio, and I play five-a-side football with Ben from the team on Thursdays, which keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool for searching documents and that's it, no drama. That's probably what most lawyers at the firm would say. I'd say it fairly, because I've used it and it does help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the plain version touches my job, because disclosure is exactly the routine screen work it speeds up. If the software finds the key emails in a day instead of a week, the firm bills fewer junior hours. My hours target doesn't go down, so I'd have to find other work to fill it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham for more drafting and more time in hearings, so my day isn't only document review. I'd use the review software on every case where the client allows it, to get quicker at it. And I'd keep saving about £250 a month, because my rent is due to go up and I've only got about three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but the part of it I'm paid for is getting smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the job would you most like more of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advocacy, which means standing up in court and arguing the case. Juniors at our firm do the small hearings, like asking a judge for more time. I'd volunteer for every small hearing I could get. Standing up in front of a judge is the part of the job a computer can't do for me yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The contract reviewers we bring in on big cases, who are paid by the hour just to read documents. They're often lawyers too, waiting for a permanent job. If the software gets better, they're the first to stop getting calls.

say: AI is a **decent search tool** for documents, with no drama.
I've used it, and it **does help** with review.
think: Even plain AI speeds up **disclosure**, the part of my job that bills.
Fewer **junior hours** billed, but my **target** stays the same.
do: Ask my supervisor for more **drafting** and **hearing** work.
Use the **review software** on every case that allows it.
Keep saving **£250 a month** before my rent rises.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the part I'm paid for is **shrinking**.
S0.quote: I'd volunteer for every small hearing I could get. Standing up in front of a judge is the part of the job a computer can't do for me yet.
fieldNote: He sees that even the mild scenario touches his **document review** hours.
His instinct is to move toward **advocacy**, the in-person part of the job.
His cushion is thin-ish at **three months**, with a rent rise coming.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor for small hearings and more drafting work
Use the firm's AI review software on every allowed case
Save £250 a month before the rent rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and firms should be honest with juniors about what it means for training and jobs. I'd say it to the partners if asked, and to my mates at football. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think disclosure as a job for juniors basically ends. Checking, writing first drafts and answering client emails are all on that card, and that's two-thirds of what I do. The firm will still need some juniors, but fewer, and they'll want the ones who are good on their feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the firm's AI training once a few of the others had tried it and said it's worth it, maybe in the second month. I'd sign up for the advocacy course that lets solicitors appear in higher courts, about £2,000, and ask the firm to pay half. And I'd cut back on eating out to get my savings from three months to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a busy kind of anxious. There's something to do, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for others to try the training first. Why not go straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen it before. The first version of every system at my firm is a mess. I'd let the keen colleagues find the problems, then learn the version that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm fine but I'm changing what I focus on, because they'd worry otherwise. My dad drives a bus and he'd ask if I should have done something with my hands. I'd tell him maybe, and we'd laugh about it, but he'd have a point.

say: Firms should be **honest with juniors** about training and jobs.
It's a **big change**, and I'd say so to the partners.
think: Disclosure as a **junior job** basically ends.
The firm keeps **fewer juniors**, mostly the ones good on their feet.
do: Join the firm's **AI training** in the second month, once others have tried it.
Take the **higher courts advocacy** course, about **£2,000**.
Cut eating out to grow savings from **three to five months**.
feel: **Anxious**, but a **busy kind** of anxious with things to do.
S1.quote: The first version of every system at my firm is a mess. I'd let the keen colleagues find the problems, then learn the version that works.
fieldNote: He expects his **team to shrink** and knows he isn't the strongest junior.
His bet is **advocacy**, which keeps him in the courtroom.
He learns tech **second wave**, after others test it, which fits his steady style.

steps.text: Join the firm's AI training once colleagues have tested it
Take the higher courts advocacy course and ask for half funding
Cut eating out to grow savings to five months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs a plan for millions of office workers, fast. I'd say it plainly, not angrily, because angry doesn't get anything done. I'd want to hear what the Law Society, our professional body, says before I said much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 I think a firm like mine needs a handful of partners and the AI, and not much else. Courts might still want a person standing up for a while, because judges move slowly. But I'd be one of the juniors let go, probably in the first round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food and build the savings as far as they'll go, maybe to five months. I'd apply for in-house jobs at construction companies, where knowing the industry might count for something. And I'd talk to my parents about moving back home if the job went, because the studio rent would eat everything in four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep badly, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me, because I'm at a desk. It means more for the building clients, whose site workers keep going until 2031. Builders on site would outlast the lawyers suing about their work. I'd almost find that funny, if it were someone else's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben at football that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're both in the same boat and we should keep our CVs ready. Ben would joke about becoming a football coach. Then we'd both go quiet in the car park.

say: The government needs a **plan** for millions of **office workers**.
I'd say it **plainly**, not angrily, and wait for the Law Society.
think: A firm like mine needs a **handful of partners** and the AI by 2028.
I'd be a junior **let go** in the **first round**.
do: Cut all spending except **rent and food** to stretch savings.
Apply for **in-house jobs** at construction companies.
Plan to **move back home** if the job goes.
S2.quote: Builders on site would outlast the lawyers suing about their work. I'd almost find that funny, if it were someone else's job.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** in the first round of cuts.
He sees **in-house work** at construction firms as a short bridge, not a fix.
Home with his **parents** is his real safety net, given high studio rent.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent and food
Apply for in-house legal jobs at construction companies
Arrange to move back to his parents' home if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for firms to retrain people properly, so they should start now. I'd ask in our team meeting what the firm's plan is for juniors. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have about four useful years, and then the firm would shrink a lot. If I've got advocacy rights by then, I might be one of the people who still goes to court. I'm not sure, but it's a better bet than staying on disclosure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the higher courts advocacy course in the first year. I'd ask for a move to the team that does mediations and settlement meetings, where you deal with people face to face. And I'd keep saving, aiming for six months by 2029, around £300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less so than with two years. There's a path, it's just narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you're not one of the people kept, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at the courts themselves, maybe a job as a tribunal clerk or a junior judge's assistant, because those public jobs might move slower. I'd take a pay cut. I'd rather earn less in a court office than earn nothing while I wait for the firm to call me back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any big personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd been thinking about buying a flat in about three years. I'd probably keep renting and wait, because I don't want a mortgage I can't pay in 2031. I'd hate it, but it's the sensible thing.

say: Five years is enough for **proper retraining**.
Firms should **start now** and tell juniors the plan.
I'd ask the **team meeting** what the firm plans for its juniors.
think: I'd have **four useful years**, then the firm shrinks.
**Advocacy rights** might make me one of the people still in court.
do: Complete the **higher courts advocacy** course in the first year.
Ask to move to the **mediation and settlement** team.
Save about **£300 a month** to reach six months by **2029**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a **narrow path** that I can see.
S3.quote: I'd rather earn less in a court office than earn nothing while I wait for the firm to call me back.
fieldNote: He expects the firm to **shrink a lot** but sees a narrow way through **advocacy**.
He'd **delay buying a flat**, a sensible-but-resented choice.
His fallback is a **public court job**, which he believes moves slower.

steps.text: Complete the higher courts advocacy course this year
Save £300 a month towards six months of costs
Keep renting and postpone buying a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and lawyers should use it, not panic. I'd tell younger trainees to get into court early. I'd keep the same calm line at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for the next few years, and by 2036 I'd be 37 with maybe ten years of court experience. That's either very valuable or not at all, depending on whether courts still want people. I'd honestly give it even odds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal for the first year and use the review software when it helps. I'd do the advocacy course within two years. And I'd buy the flat after all, because ten years is longer than most mortgages are fixed for, and I'd have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks safe for now, but I'd always have one eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even odds. What tips it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether people still trust a judge's decision if a machine wrote the argument. If people still want a person to argue their case in court, I'm useful. If they don't, ten years of court experience is worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I've got a decade to work it out, and that's longer than he had when the bus company changed its routes and half the drivers went. He'd tell me to stop worrying and go to football. He's usually right.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, so lawyers shouldn't panic.
Young trainees should **get into court** early.
I'd keep the same **calm line** at work as I do now.
think: I'm **fine** for the next few years.
My court experience is **very valuable** or worthless, with **even odds**.
do: Carry on as normal and use the **review software** when it helps.
Finish the **advocacy course** within two years.
Buy the **flat** after all, with time to adjust.
feel: **Uneasy**, with **one eye** always on the job.
S4.quote: If people still want a person to argue their case in court, I'm useful. If they don't, ten years of court experience is worth nothing.
fieldNote: With ten years he feels **safe for now** and goes ahead with the **flat**.
He frames the future as a **coin toss** over whether courts want people.
His dad's experience of **bus route cuts** shapes how he talks about change.

steps.text: Keep working in litigation and use review software when it helps
Finish the higher courts advocacy course within two years
Buy a flat with a long fixed-rate mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be let go in the first round with three months of savings. What would help is the government paying people's rent for a while, and the professional body helping lawyers move into court and public jobs. Something concrete, not a website with tips.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people's parents did. My dad drives a bus and saw half the drivers go when the routes changed. He thinks a law degree means I'm safe, and I don't correct him. I think that shapes how we all react to this.

headlineQuote: My dad drives a bus and saw half the drivers go when the routes changed. He thinks a law degree means I'm safe, and I don't correct him.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** litigation junior who spends most days on **document review** for building disputes.
He's **steady**: he learns the tools once others have tested them.
His plan in every picture is to move toward **advocacy** and face-to-face work.
He expects to be **let go early** if AGI comes fast, and would move back home.
With ten years, he feels **safe enough** to buy a flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when he'd be cut early with only three months saved.
whatWouldHelp: Government **rent support** for a while after a job loss.
Help from the **professional body** moving lawyers into court and public jobs.
